notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: Democrats' talk of a data-centre moratorium has cut share prices across Asia, where growth now rests on building AI.

watch.what: A US state, county or city pauses, rejects or puts power or water conditions on a data-centre project after the midterms.
watch.because: If markets are pricing a political limit on the AI build, the first limits should come from local and state bodies, not from a Congress that still faces a Trump veto.

watch.what: The Nasdaq is reported to have recovered at least half of its post-election fall.
watch.because: The join says the fall priced a federal moratorium that cannot become law while Trump can veto it, so the national part of the fall should reverse while local limits remain.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the spring of 2000, when the Nasdaq fell from its March peak and Taiwanese and Korean technology shares, which had risen on the same internet spending, fell with it; the Nasdaq lost 78% by October 2002. The difference is that the companies now doing the spending earn large profits, and the threat named in these headlines is political, a limit on permits, power and water, rather than a collapse in demand.

paths.name: Building moves to friendlier states
paths.text: The call for a national moratorium stalls over the coming months, because any bill needs Trump's signature until January 2029. The fight moves to state utility regulators and county councils, and companies place new sites in Republican-run states such as Wyoming and abroad. Markets recover much of the post-election fall, and Asian suppliers trade on each local decision.
paths.sign: A large AI company says it is moving or adding a data-centre site in another state after a local rejection.

paths.name: A longer AI correction
paths.text: The sell-off exposes how much of the build depends on borrowing, lenders tighten terms and the large builders trim next year's spending. Taiwanese and Korean shares fall further and Korean investors who borrowed against their shares are forced to sell. This is less likely because the largest builders pay mostly from their own cash.
paths.sign: A large cloud company cuts its capital spending guidance for next year.

paths.name: Congress limits the build
paths.text: Democrats attach data-centre conditions to a funding bill that Trump must sign to avoid a shutdown. This is unlikely before the new Congress sits in January, and Trump has tied his economic case to AI.
paths.sign: A federal funding bill passes with a clause on data-centre power or water use.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the AI build is likely to become a permitting question decided state by state and country by country, with power and water as the deciding terms, and East Asia's export economies will stay tied to whoever grants those permits.

readings.claim: After their midterm sweep, senior Democrats called for a national moratorium on data centres, and on the same day the Nasdaq fell more than 5%, US retail traders sold the most stock since the Covid crash, foreign investors sold NT$102.4bn of Taiwanese shares, Japanese and Korean stocks fell and the Brazilian real weakened. Several of these headlines name the Democratic win and the fear of a slower AI build as the cause. The selling reached furthest into the markets whose recent growth comes from supplying that build, while an Indian banker said the same news made India more attractive. A US vote about local power and water has become a price in Taipei, Tokyo and Seoul because those markets are now largely a bet on American data centres.

events.label: Democrats call for data-centre moratorium
Wall Street's tech sell-off after the vote
Asian and Israeli shares fall
Brazilian real weakens on risk aversion
Indian shares pitched as the alternative
Data-centre building and AI adoption continue

rungs.label: The vote and the US sell-off

fragments.label: A moratorium is proposed
fragments.text: CNBC in the United States reports top Democrats calling for a 'national data center moratorium now' after the midterm sweep, and in a second piece says voters rejected data centres over resource concerns and that their water use is hard to measure. bdnews24 in Bangladesh puts the Nasdaq 100 on course for a $1.8tn loss as the Democratic win raises fears of AI delays.

fragments.label: Wall Street falls
fragments.text: Al-Anbaa in Lebanon, citing Reuters, reports the S&P 500 down 4.1%, the Nasdaq down 5.4% and the Dow down 3.2%. CNBC says retail traders sold more stock in a single day than at any time since the Covid sell-off. Habertürk in Turkey calls it an AI earthquake, Youm7 in Egypt says Elon Musk lost $60bn after the Republican defeat, and Diário do Grande ABC in Brazil says tech stocks led the fall after the elections.

fragments.label: Asian and Israeli markets
fragments.text: ETtoday in Taiwan reports foreign investors sold NT$102.4bn of Taiwanese shares in a day. Nikkan Gendai in Japan says the midterms hit the Tokyo market directly and asks whether the AI rally collapses and the Nikkei falls below 60,000. Financial News in South Korea reports major shareholders who borrowed 170bn won against their shares unable to sleep as prices drop. nbd.com.cn in China reports FTSE China A50 futures down 1.85% overnight, and Globes in Israel reports defence and tech stocks tumbling.

fragments.label: A currency and a rotation
fragments.text: Diário do Grande ABC reports the dollar rising to R$5.48 as risk aversion spreads with the tech sell-off. BusinessLine in India quotes Uday Kotak saying Indian equities gain appeal as concerns over AI spending ease. The same news is a loss in one emerging market and a sales pitch in another.

rungs.label: One build priced in many markets

fragments.label: Why Asia sold together
fragments.text: The join is that a large share of the value in Taipei, Seoul and Tokyo now rests on a single programme of spending: data centres built mainly in the United States. A congressional threat to that programme is a threat to the Taiwanese foundries, Korean memory makers and Japanese suppliers who fill it, so they were sold on the same day for the same reason. India, whose market holds little AI hardware, read the same news as good for itself, which is what the join predicts.

fragments.label: The build itself carries on
fragments.text: On the same day Anadolu in Turkey reports Google committing $17bn to its first data centre in Wyoming, a Republican-run state, and Yicai in China reports Tencent's WorkBuddy office tool grew tenfold. The sell-off is about where and on what terms the build happens in the United States, not about whether companies still want it. That makes it a political price rather than a judgement on the technology.

fragments.label: A normal repricing with several causes
fragments.text: One day's fall after an election is ordinary, and valuations in Tokyo and Seoul were already high enough to fall on any news. Globes reports Israeli defence stocks falling alongside tech, which points to hopes of the Iran war ending rather than to data centres. The events part where it matters: the Brazilian real weakened because investors bought dollars in general, the Israeli fall mixes war and tech, and the Indian comment is a banker promoting his own market. The moratorium call comes from party leaders who cannot pass it, so markets may simply have overreacted to words.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: ChatGPT's release on 30 November 2022 turned a research field into a spending programme. By 2025 Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were each spending tens of billions of dollars a year on data centres, and Nvidia became the most valuable company in the world. That spending ran through Asian supply chains: TSMC in Taiwan made the chips, SK Hynix and Samsung in Korea made the high-bandwidth memory, and Japanese firms supplied materials and tools. At the same time the sites became local politics. Residents in Virginia, Georgia and Arizona argued over power bills and water, and in November 2025 Democrats won seats on Georgia's utility regulator after a campaign about electricity prices. By these headlines, voters in 2026 turned against data centres over resource concerns and Democratic leaders now call for a national moratorium. That is the step from a county argument to a national one, and it is why foreign investors sold NT$102.4bn of Taiwanese shares in a day.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, the Federal Reserve held its rate near zero for seven years and bought trillions of dollars of bonds. Cheap money and the smartphone together made a handful of platform companies the largest firms in the world; by 2024 seven of them made up about a third of the S&P 500's value. The second change was who owned shares. Commission-free apps such as Robinhood in the United States, and the wave of Korean small investors known as the 'Donghak ants' during the 2020 crash, brought millions of households into the market, many of them on borrowed money. That is why one day's news now travels so far. CNBC reports retail traders selling more than on any day since the Covid sell-off, and Korean major shareholders who borrowed 170bn won against their holdings face margin calls. A decade of concentration means that a vote about one industry moves the whole index.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The Asian side of this sell-off was built after the Cold War. Morris Chang founded TSMC in 1987 with Taiwanese state backing to make chips designed by others, and in the 1990s Korea's conglomerates bet heavily on memory. China's opening after 1992 and the founding of the WTO in 1995 joined these firms into one supply chain serving American demand. Netscape's listing in August 1995 showed that a technology could be priced long before it earned. When that bubble burst in March 2000, the Nasdaq's 78% fall was matched by heavy falls in Taipei and Seoul, because they made the hardware. The lesson then was that East Asia's exporters carry American technology risk one step removed. Nikkan Gendai asking whether a US election sends the Nikkei below 60,000 is the same exposure, though the risk named now is a permit rather than a business model.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The postwar order produced both halves of this story. The United States paid for computing as a state project: the Dartmouth workshop named artificial intelligence in 1956, and after Sputnik in 1957 the new research agency ARPA funded the work that became the internet. Washington also underwrote the industries of its Asian allies, opening its market to Japanese goods and protecting Taiwan and South Korea while they built export manufacturing under state direction from the 1960s. For sixty years the pace of new technology was set in federal budgets. The AI build reversed that arrangement: it is privately funded, and the state's part is the permit, the grid connection and the water licence. When Democrats call for a national moratorium and Google announces $17bn in Wyoming on the same day, the question is again what the American state will allow, and the allies' markets still move on the answer.

readings.line: The war's oil price now pushes rates up in countries that buy oil, while central banks in countries that sell it cut.

watch.what: The Bank of Korea or the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raises its rate at its late-November meeting and names oil or the Iran war.
watch.because: Both countries import nearly all their oil, so if trade position decides the response they should follow London rather than Mexico City.

watch.what: Bangladesh announces a fuel or gas price rise, new import curbs or a request to the IMF to protect reserves now below $30bn.
watch.because: The join says importers without a strong currency pay the war's price in reserves, which forces a choice between domestic prices and dollars within weeks.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is 2008, when oil reached $147 a barrel in July and the European Central Bank raised its rate to 4.25% against the price, while oil exporters' budgets filled. Within three months Lehman Brothers had failed and the ECB was cutting. The difference now is that the price comes from a war and a closed strait rather than from strong demand, so it could fall quickly on a deal, and Brazil and Mexico start from much higher rates.

paths.name: Importers keep raising into the new year
paths.text: The Bank of England has said this rise will not be the last, and other importing central banks follow in November and December. Bangladesh and similar importers raise fuel prices or seek IMF money as reserves fall. This holds as long as the strait stays closed, and nothing in these headlines suggests that ends within weeks.
paths.sign: A second oil-importing central bank raises its rate and names the war.

paths.name: A deal lowers oil and rates
paths.text: Iran's proposal sent through Qatar becomes an agreement before the end of the year, oil falls toward the lower price Indonesia projects for next year, and the Bank of England's rise is its only one. Talks have stalled before, which is why this is not the favoured path.
paths.sign: Brent crude is reported falling 10% in a week on news of a US-Iran agreement.

paths.name: Exporters forced to raise
paths.text: The tech sell-off and wider risk aversion push the real and the peso down far enough that Brazil and Mexico reverse course and raise. Unlikely because oil revenue supports both currencies and both banks have room after cutting.
paths.sign: Brazil's Copom raises the Selic rate and cites the exchange rate.

ahead.decade: Over ten years a recurring Gulf risk is likely to keep oil-importing countries building reserves and alternative energy at a cost to growth, while exporters outside the Gulf gain room, a sorting of monetary policy by energy position that the move away from oil will narrow only slowly.

readings.change: The previous edition had central banks abroad holding rates high against the war's price. Today the Bank of England went further and raised to 4%, saying more could follow if the war continues. But Mexico's and Brazil's central banks cut on the same day, so holding high no longer describes rate-setters in general.
readings.claim: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4%, its first rise since 2023, and warned of more if the Iran war continues, on the day Mexico's central bank cut to 6.25% and Brazil's continued to cut. Russia records its highest oil and gas revenue and a central bank warning of overheating, while Bangladesh's reserves fall below $30bn as its fuel import bill doubles. The oil price is the same for every country, but what it does to money depends on whether a country buys or sells oil. Buyers are paying in higher rates and lost reserves, and sellers have room to cut.

events.label: Bank of England raises rates to 4%
Mexico and Brazil cut rates
Russia's record oil revenue and overheating
Bangladesh's reserves fall on fuel imports
Oil and power costs hit other importers
Indonesia expects cheaper oil next year

fragments.label: London raises
fragments.text: The Bournemouth Echo in Britain reports the Bank raising rates to 4% and warning of more if the Iran war continues. Business Day in South Africa and La Tercera in Chile call it the first rise since 2023. Newspim in South Korea, whose headline as rendered names the Bank of Korea but quotes Governor Bailey saying the rise will not be the last, is reporting the same British decision.

fragments.label: Mexico and Brazil cut
fragments.text: La Razón de México reports Banxico cutting its rate to 6.25%. Diário do Grande ABC in Brazil reports rates falling, with the yield curve shifting after a less cautious Copom statement. Neither headline mentions the war.

fragments.label: Russia's revenue
fragments.text: Kommersant reports record federal oil and gas revenue in October. Izvestia reports the central bank recording an overheating economy in the third quarter. Kommersant also reports Russian imports of petroleum products up 25% in October.

fragments.label: Importers' bills
fragments.text: The Daily Star in Bangladesh reports the trade deficit widening 31% as the fuel import bill doubles, and bdnews24 reports reserves below $30bn after a $1.64bn Asian Clearing Union payment; dhakaToday reports a torch march in Chattogram demanding a gas price cut. Channel Africa says the oil shock hits developing economies hardest, Kenya Today cites a World Bank update on high power costs threatening Kenyan industry, and Sky TG24 in Italy reports Istat data on rising prices and emptier shopping baskets.

rungs.label: How trade position sets the rate

fragments.label: A transfer from buyers to sellers
fragments.text: A higher oil price moves money from countries that buy oil to countries that sell it. In Britain it arrives as inflation the central bank must answer, in Bangladesh as dollars leaving the reserves, and in the selling countries as revenue that supports the currency and the budget, which leaves Banxico and the Copom free to cut. Russia shows the far end of the selling side, where revenue is large enough that the central bank worries about overheating.

fragments.label: Domestic reasons, and imperfect sellers
fragments.text: Mexico and Brazil may be cutting for their own reasons: both started from high real rates and slowing growth, and Mexico buys much of its petrol from the United States, so it is not a clean seller. Russia's 25% rise in fuel imports shows that a crude exporter can still be short of fuel. Republika in Indonesia projects oil falling next year, so any split may be brief. The events part on a basic point: the British decision names the war, and the Mexican and Brazilian headlines name nothing of it.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The inflation that followed the pandemic set the terms for this decision. The Bank of England raised its rate fourteen times, from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed British energy bills to records, and then cut. Brazil's central bank, which began raising in March 2021, took the Selic to 15% by mid-2025, while Banxico cut from its 11.25% peak as Mexican inflation fell. Central banks learned in those years that waiting to see whether an energy shock was temporary cost them credibility. In June 2025 American bombers struck Fordow and ended a twelve-day war; by these headlines a wider war with Iran and the closing of Hormuz followed in 2026. The Bank of England's warning that more rises will come if the war continues is a central bank declining to wait a second time, while Brazil and Mexico use the room their earlier high rates gave them.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 the map of who sells oil changed. Shale drilling made the United States the largest producer by 2018, and in 2014 the price more than halved when OPEC chose not to cut. Brazil developed the pre-salt fields found off its coast in 2006 and 2007, and Mexico opened its oil sector in the 2013 energy reform. Russia, under sanctions after 2014, adopted a fiscal rule in 2017 to save revenue above a set price, which is why Kommersant can report record oil and gas income while the central bank warns of overheating. The Gulf meanwhile became the main risk: the Iran nuclear agreement of 2015 was abandoned by Washington in 2018, and drones halved Saudi output at Abqaiq in September 2019. Producers outside the strait gained from each scare. The war has made that gain large enough to appear in their rate decisions.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: Most of today's central banks were shaped in the 1990s. Mexico gave Banxico autonomy in 1994, the year of the peso crisis. Brazil ended hyperinflation with the Plano Real in 1994 and adopted an inflation target in 1999, and the Bank of England gained operational independence in May 1997. The Asian crisis of 1997 and Russia's default of 1998 taught importing countries that dollars held in reserve are their only defence against capital leaving at once. In 2002 the real lost a third of its value before Lula's election, and Brazil's central bank has since treated the exchange rate as something it must answer. Bangladesh learned the same lesson later: its reserves peaked near $48bn in 2021 and it took a $4.7bn IMF loan in 2023. The reserves now reported below $30bn after an Asian Clearing Union payment are that defence being spent.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The order of 1945 priced oil in dollars and tied Gulf supply to American protection. Bretton Woods fixed currencies to the dollar in 1944, and Roosevelt met Ibn Saud on the Great Bitter Lake in February 1945. When the Arab embargo of October 1973 quadrupled the price, it showed that a regional war becomes a transfer of money from buying countries to selling ones. Britain answered with high rates and, in 1976, an IMF loan, while producers placed their surplus in Western banks that lent it to Latin America until Mexico's default in 1982. Daniel Yergin's The Prize tells that history with oil as the organising fact of the century. The present split follows the same line: the Bank of England, in a country that has imported oil again since 2005, raising rates, and Bangladesh paying in reserves, while sellers bank the difference.

readings.line: Parliaments are refusing governments' budgets, so next year's tax and spending are set in the chamber rather than the cabinet.

watch.what: Another national parliament outside France and Senegal votes down or forces withdrawal of a government's budget or main tax bill.
watch.because: If legislatures now set budgets rather than approve them, the refusals should not stop at two countries in one autumn.

watch.what: France's government drops or rewrites a named tax or spending measure to win votes for its budget.
watch.because: The join says the chamber now decides, and the favoured path is concession rather than force, which would show first where the rejection was unanimous.

ahead.precedent: In December 2024 Michel Barnier forced France's social security budget through with Article 49.3 and was brought down by a censure motion on 4 December, the first French government to fall that way since 1962. A special law carried spending into 2025, and François Bayrou passed a budget in February 2025 after concessions to the Socialists. The difference now is that the rejection was unanimous, it came with nationwide wage strikes, and legislatures in Senegal, the Netherlands and the United States are resisting at the same time.

paths.name: Budgets pass late, by concession
paths.text: Between December and February the French, Dutch and Senegalese budgets pass after governments give up named measures, with stopgap laws covering the gap. Governments prefer concession because forcing a budget risks the fall Barnier suffered. In Washington a short-term funding bill carries the government into the new Congress.
paths.sign: A government announces it is dropping a tax rise or spending cut to win budget votes.

paths.name: A government falls on its budget
paths.text: A censure motion in France, or a lost vote elsewhere, brings down a government before Christmas. Possible because no deputy voted for the French budget and the strikes are large.
paths.sign: A censure motion against the French government passes.

paths.name: Budgets forced through unchanged
paths.text: Governments use decrees or constitutional procedures to pass budgets as written. Unlikely because the cost of doing so in France was shown in 2024.
paths.sign: France's government passes its budget by Article 49.3 without changes.

ahead.decade: Over ten years, with fragmented party systems and high debt, budgets in many democracies are likely to be set by shifting coalitions in the chamber, making fiscal policy slower and more often provisional than when finance ministries wrote it alone.

readings.claim: French deputies unanimously rejected their government's budget ahead of nationwide strikes for higher wages, Senegal's parliament asked for the 2027 budget bill to be withdrawn, Rob Jetten warned Dutch MPs that voting down his tax plan would cost billions, Japan's prime minister faces a time-limited committee session over a consumption tax cut, and a Democratic Congress must now fund the US government. In each case the government has proposed next year's taxes and spending and the legislature, not the cabinet, is deciding what passes. The common condition is that governments no longer command the chambers they answer to, either because they lack a majority or because their own members will not follow.

events.label: French deputies reject the budget
Wage strikes and marches in France
Senegal's parliament asks for budget withdrawal
Dutch tax plan faces defeat
Japan's consumption tax cut in committee
New Congress inherits US funding fight

fragments.label: France and Senegal
fragments.text: CNBC reports the French budget unanimously rejected by lawmakers ahead of nationwide strikes, and France Inter asks what political answer can follow the 5 November mobilisations. Sud Ouest reports the Dordogne prefect facing dozens of mayors angry at the state. Channel Africa reports Senegal's parliament requesting the withdrawal of the 2027 budget bill.

fragments.label: The Netherlands, Japan, the United States
fragments.text: Nieuws.nl reports Jetten saying that voting down his tax plan would cost billions. Nikkan Gendai in Japan calls the consumption tax cut a farce and reports that Prime Minister Takaichi will answer questions in committee on the 6th with a one-hour limit. Fortune says Congress's first task after the midterms is to keep the US government funded, before the $40tn debt is addressed.

fragments.label: Marches for higher wages
fragments.text: NOS in the Netherlands reports France protesting again for higher wages while the government tries to prevent unrest. La Dépêche reports tear gas, damaged shops and an attempt to reach the ring road in Toulouse. ENIKOS in Greece reports Alexis Tsipras marching in Paris and saying France is resisting policies that are breaking society apart.

fragments.label: The chamber decides
fragments.text: These are different budgets answering the same question, who decides next year's taxes, in the same way. In France a unanimous rejection means not one deputy, including the government's own supporters, voted for the plan. In Senegal the request to withdraw comes from a chamber in which the governing party has a large majority, so the refusal is from inside the government's own camp.

fragments.label: Cuts and tax cuts alike
fragments.text: The refusals are not only of austerity. In Japan the argument is over a tax cut the government promised, in the Netherlands over a tax plan, and in the United States over whether the government is funded at all. What moves to the chamber is the decision itself, whichever direction it takes.

fragments.label: An ordinary budget season
fragments.text: Autumn is when most budgets are voted, and rejections at first reading are common; in France the government still has constitutional tools to pass a budget. Senegal's request may be about debt figures and the IMF rather than about who holds power. The cases part sharply: France has a chamber with no majority, Senegal a majority party pressing its own executive, Japan a government arguing over its own campaign promise, and the United States a divided government after an election. Only the French and Senegalese cases are outright refusals.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: Pandemic spending raised public debt across the rich world and left less room in each following budget. Then majorities went. Macron lost his majority in June 2022, and his snap election of July 2024 produced an assembly with no workable majority; Michel Barnier and François Bayrou both lost office over budgets within a year. In the Netherlands the Schoof cabinet collapsed in June 2025 and D66 under Rob Jetten came first in the October 2025 election. Japan's Liberal Democrats lost their lower house majority in October 2024 and their upper house majority in July 2025, so Sanae Takaichi governs by deals and a consumption tax cut became part of the price. Washington had its longest shutdown, 43 days, in late 2025. Senegal's new government found in 2024 that past debt had been understated, and the IMF paused lending. By these headlines, each budget this autumn meets a chamber its cabinet cannot count on.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The fragmentation of the chambers began with the austerity after 2008. In the euro crisis, budgets were written with bond markets and creditors at the table: Greece signed its first bailout in May 2010, and voters who rejected its terms built new parties. Spain's indignados camped in the Puerta del Sol in May 2011 and their movement became Podemos. In Greece, Syriza under Alexis Tsipras won in January 2015 and held a referendum against the creditors' terms that July. Adam Tooze's Crashed traces how a financial crisis became a decade of politics. The centre parties that had passed budgets alone for decades lost their share, in France as elsewhere: in 2017 neither the Socialists nor the Republicans reached the presidential run-off. Tsipras marching in Paris against policies he says are breaking society apart links the austerity of the 2010s directly to this autumn's budget fight.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The fiscal rules these budgets answer to date from the years after the Cold War. The Maastricht treaty of 1992 set the 3% deficit limit that French and Dutch budgets are still judged against, and the euro's launch in 1999 removed devaluation as a way out. Senegal's rules come from the West African Economic and Monetary Union, created in January 1994 in the same month the CFA franc was devalued by half, which binds its budget to regional deficit ceilings and to the IMF's view of its debt. Japan introduced its consumption tax in April 1989 at 3%, raised it to 5% in 1997, 8% in 2014 and 10% in 2019, and each rise cost or nearly cost a government its standing. The committee session Nikkan Gendai calls a farce is the latest argument over a tax that has shaped Japanese elections for thirty-seven years.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The postwar welfare states made the budget the main thing a parliament decides, and France wrote its constitution around the danger of that. The Fourth Republic had more than twenty governments in twelve years, many of them brought down over money, so the constitution of 1958 gave the government Article 49.3, which passes a bill unless the assembly removes the government. Wage claims were settled outside parliament: in May 1968 ten million strikers won the Grenelle agreements, which raised the minimum wage by 35%. Tony Judt's Postwar describes how that settlement depended on growth that paid for both wages and services. The 5 November marches for higher wages and a budget rejected without a single vote in favour test both arrangements at once, with workers asking for more and deputies refusing to pass a plan for less.

readings.line: Governments now send soldiers to keep ordinary civil order at home, and police seek rules on force closer to a soldier's.

watch.what: Indonesia's government or armed forces say the troop deployment in Jakarta will continue or widen beyond its first stated period.
watch.because: If soldiers are becoming a standing part of civil order rather than a one-off measure, deployments should be extended rather than ended.

watch.what: France's National Assembly or Senate votes to pass the bill widening when police may use firearms.
watch.because: The join says domestic force is moving toward military rules from both directions, so the government should press the bill despite opposition from the left.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is Mexico from December 2006, when Felipe Calderón sent the army against the drug cartels as a temporary measure. The soldiers were never withdrawn: a National Guard was created in 2019 under civilian command and moved to the defence ministry by constitutional change in 2024. The present deployments are smaller, and they are in countries such as Indonesia and Bangladesh whose transitions to democracy were defined by removing soldiers from civil life.

paths.name: Deployments become standing arrangements
paths.text: Over the next year the Jakarta deployment, Bangladesh's joint forces and Pakistan's election duty are extended and written into decrees or standing orders, because governments that distrust their police find soldiers easier to command. Few will be announced as permanent, but few will end.
paths.sign: A government extends an army deployment on domestic duty by decree.

paths.name: A killing forces a pull-back
paths.text: Soldiers on civil duty kill protesters or bystanders, and a court or parliament orders them back to barracks. Possible given the death in the Aceh riot.
paths.sign: A court or parliament orders soldiers withdrawn from a city or from election duty.

paths.name: Police reform replaces soldiers
paths.text: Governments invest in civilian police and withdraw the troops. Unlikely within a year because police reform takes longer than a budget cycle.
paths.sign: A government names a police recruitment or reform programme as the reason for withdrawing troops.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the line drawn in the transitions of the 1990s between soldiers and police is likely to keep moving back toward the soldier in middle-income democracies, with courts the main place where it is contested.

readings.claim: Indonesia's armed forces commander has put troops in Jakarta and the army has given its own account of a deadly riot at a Maulid celebration in Aceh; Pakistan has deployed the army and Rangers for by-elections in Punjab; a Bangladeshi soldier was killed raiding human traffickers at Teknaf; and Lebanon's army ran raids and checkpoints that led to dozens of arrests. In France, a bill widening when police may fire was called a major advance by police unions and a licence to kill by the left. In each case a job that civilian police once did, or were meant to do alone, is being handed to soldiers or to rules closer to theirs.

events.label: Troops deployed in Jakarta
Army's account of the Aceh riot
Army and Rangers guard Punjab by-elections
Soldier killed in Teknaf trafficking raid
Lebanese army raids and checkpoints
French bill on police firearms use

fragments.label: Indonesia
fragments.text: Republika reports the armed forces commander, on deploying TNI personnel in Jakarta, saying they stand ready to defend the unitary state from various threats. Viva reports Aceh calm again and the TNI giving details of the riot at a Maulid celebration that killed one resident. In both, the army rather than the police is the voice of public order.

fragments.label: Pakistan, Bangladesh, Lebanon
fragments.text: SAMAA TV reports the army and Rangers deployed for by-elections in Punjab. bdnews24 reports a soldier killed and army personnel injured in gunfire with human traffickers during a joint forces raid in Teknaf. Al-Anbaa in Lebanon reports raids and army checkpoints in several areas, with dozens arrested and weapons seized.

fragments.label: A bill on firing
fragments.text: Réunion La 1ère reports a bill on the legitimate use of firearms by law enforcement, described as a major advance by police unions and a licence to kill by the left. Here no soldiers are involved. The civilian police are being given wider latitude to use lethal force instead.

fragments.label: The same answer in different places
fragments.text: These are separate decisions about the same question, who carries force inside the country, and they are being answered the same way: with the institution that has more weapons and fewer limits. Indonesia and Bangladesh both cut back their armies' domestic roles after their democratic transitions, so troops in Jakarta and joint forces at Teknaf are a reversal there, not a continuation. France reaches the same point from the other side, by writing rules for its police that come closer to those for soldiers.

fragments.label: Votes and frontiers first
fragments.text: The duties handed to soldiers are the ones where governments trust their police least: guarding polling stations, as in Punjab, and frontiers used by smugglers, as at Teknaf and in Lebanon. These are also the duties where a mistake has the highest political cost, which is why governments want a force that takes orders without local ties.

fragments.label: Old arrangements on one day
fragments.text: Several of these are long-standing. Pakistan's army has guarded elections for decades, Lebanon's army has long been its main internal security force, and raids at Teknaf are border work on a frontier with Myanmar rather than city policing. The Jakarta deployment may be tied to one occasion. The events do not share a task: one is election security, one a border raid, one a patrol in a capital, one an account of a riot and one a draft law about police, not soldiers. The pattern may come from a single day's sample of local outlets.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic gave soldiers a domestic job in many countries. In 2020 armies enforced lockdowns and ran vaccination centres from Peru to Indonesia, and France ran a military support operation called Résilience. The decade's uprisings then widened that role. After students forced Sheikh Hasina from Bangladesh in August 2024, many police stations were left unmanned, and in September 2024 the interim government gave army officers magistrates' powers; the joint forces at Teknaf, where a soldier was killed raiding traffickers, work under that arrangement. In March 2025 Indonesia's parliament amended the armed forces law to let serving officers hold more civilian posts, over student protests. In France the police killing of Nahel Merzouk in June 2023, under a 2017 law that loosened the rules on firing at vehicles, set the terms of the argument over the present firearms bill. Each step was presented as temporary or exceptional.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: Several of these duties grew from the movements of people after 2008. In August 2017 more than 700,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar into Cox's Bazar district, where Teknaf lies, and the camps became a base for trafficking routes by sea toward Malaysia. Lebanon took in more than a million Syrians after the war began in 2011, and its army became the force on the border and around the camps, which is the work behind the raids and checkpoints Al-Anbaa reports. Egypt in 2011 taught the decade another lesson: in Tahrir Square the army acted as arbiter between the crowd and the state, and in 2013 it took power. Governments since have treated the army as the institution that still functions when the police do not, and frontiers and camps as the places where that habit begins before it reaches the capital.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The transitions at the end of the Cold War set the rule that soldiers leave civil life. Bangladesh's military ruler Hussain Muhammad Ershad fell in December 1990 and parliamentary government returned in 1991. In Indonesia, after Suharto resigned in May 1998, the police were separated from the armed forces in 1999 and 2000, and the doctrine of dwifungsi, the army's combined military and political role, was ended. Samuel Huntington's The Third Wave counted civilian control of the army among the tests of a new democracy. Pakistan went the other way with Pervez Musharraf's coup in October 1999, and Aceh's own conflict ended only with the Helsinki agreement of 2005. The Jakarta deployment and the army's account of the Aceh riot are read in Indonesia against the 1998 settlement, and the commander's phrase about defending the unitary state is the language of the army's old domestic mission.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: In many states founded after 1945 the army existed before the constitution. Indonesia's army was formed in the war of independence against the Dutch from 1945, and General Nasution's 'middle way' doctrine of 1958 gave it a permanent political role. Pakistan's army took power in 1958 under Ayub Khan, and Bangladesh, independent in 1971, had its first coups in 1975. In those states a soldier at a polling station is familiar, and the question has always been who commands him. France answered the question differently. Its state of emergency law of April 1955, written during the Algerian war, gives civilian prefects exceptional powers, and was used again in 2005 and 2015. The police firearms bill reported from La Réunion belongs to that tradition, in which the civilian state widens its own rules on force rather than calling in troops.
